τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ ἀπέθανεν ἐφάπαξ· καὶ αὐτὸς ἀποθανὼν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ συζῇ Χριστῷ· ζῇ δὲ
Χριστῷ ὁ ἐν καινότητι ζωῆ περιπατῶν. 28 v 5–9 ὅτι ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ θεοῦ ἐκκέχυται ἐν
ταῖς καρδίαις ἡμῶν διὰ πνεύματος ἁγίου τοῦ δοθέντος ἡμῖν· ἔτι γὰρ Χριστὸς ὄντων
ἡμῶν ἀσθενῶν κατὰ καιρὸν ὑπὲρ ἀσεβῶν ἀπέθανεν· μόλις γὰρ ὑπὲρ δικαίου τις
ἀποθανεῖται· ὑπὲρ γὰρ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ τάχα τις καὶ τολμᾷ ἀποθανεῖν· συνίστησι δὲ τὴν
ἑαυτοῦ ἀγάπην εἰς ἡμᾶς ὁ θεὸς ὅτι ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν Χριστὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν
ἀπέθανεν· πολλῷ οὖν μᾶλλον δικαιωθέντες νῦν ἐν τῷ αἵματι αὐτοῦ σωθησόμεθα δι'
αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τῆς ὀργῆς. ὅπου μὲν ἀσθενεῖς ἢ ἁμαρτωλοὺς ὀνομάζει, καὶ ἑαυτὸν τοῖς
τοιούτοις ἐμπερι λαμβάνει· ὅπου δὲ λέγει ἀσεβεῖς, οὐκέτι. καὶ τάχα εἰκότως ὁ ὑπὸ
τὸν νόμον ὤν, ὃς ἠ θένει διὰ τῆ αρκό , ἀσθενὴς μέν ἐστι καὶ ἁμαρτωλός, οὐ μὴν καὶ
κατὰ τὴν συνήθειαν τῆς διαστολῆς τῶν γραφῶν καὶ ἀσεβής, λεγόντων τῶν ὑπὸ
νόμον ἁμαρτανόντων τῷ θεῷ καὶ γὰρ ἐὰν ἁμαρτάνωμεν οί ἐ μεν εἰδότε ου τὸ
κράτο · ἀσεβεῖς δὲ τότε οἱ νομιζόμενοι εἶναι ὑπὸ τὸν νόμον τυγχάνουσιν, ἐπὰν
ἐγκαταλιπόντες τὸν θεὸν τῶν πατέρων ζητοῦσι τοὺς θεοὺς τῶν ἐθνῶν. πρὶν δὲ
προσελθεῖν ἡμᾶς θεοσεβείᾳ ἀγάπη ἐν ἡμῖν οὐ συνειστήκει, πάντα γὰρ μᾶλλον ἢ θεὸν
ἀγαπῶμεν· ὅτε δὲ τοιούτων ἡμῶν ὑπαρχόντων Χριστὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀπέθανε, τότε
συνέστη καὶ ὑπέστη ἐν ἡμῖν ἡ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀγάπη, πάντων περιαιρεθέντων τῷ τοῦ
Ἰησοῦ θανάτῳ ἀφ' ἡμῶν τῶν ἐμποδιζόντων τῇ συστάσει τῆς εἰς ἡμᾶς τοῦ θεοῦ
ἀγάπης. κατὰ ταύτην οὖν τὴν διήγησιν τοῦ συνίστησιν ἀκουστέον, συνιστάντος καὶ
ὑφιστάντος τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν ἡμῖν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἀγάπην, τὴν οὐδενὸς ἑτέρου κυρίως ἢ
αὐτοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ τυγχάνουσαν. (Ὠριγενοῦς) [οὐ γὰρ μόνον τὴν ἀθάνατον ζωὴν
ἀναμένομεν, ἀλλὰ καὶ κατὰ τὸν παρόντα βίον ὡς προσοικειωθέντες τῷ θεῷ
σεμνυνόμεθα, τὰ κατὰ τὸν δεσπότην Χριστὸν λογιζόμενοι, ὃς μεσίτης ἡμῶν
γενόμενος τὴν εἰρήνην ἐπραγματεύσατο.] 29 vi 5 εἰ γὰρ σύμφυτοι γεγόναμεν τῷ
ὁμοιώματι τοῦ θανάτου αὐτοῦ, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως ἐσόμεθα. πλάσας τὸ ὄνομα
τέθεικεν, φυτόν τι ἐπιστάμενος τὸν Ἰησοῦ θάνατον, φέρον κάρπους ἀναιρετικοὺς
τῆς ἁμαρτίας· ᾧ φυτῷ ὁ λόγος γεωργεῖ ἐν τοῖς παρα δεξαμένοις τὴν διδασκαλίαν τὴν
διὰ Χριστοῦ, ποιῶν αὐτοὺς συμφύτους τῷ ὁμοιώματι τοῦ θανάτου· ὁμοίωμα μὲν γάρ
τι τοῦ θανάτου ἐκείνου δύναται ἡ ἀνθρωπίνη φύσις ἀναλαβεῖν, τὸν δὲ ἐκείνου
θάνατον τοῦ ἁμαρτίαν μὴ ποιή αντο , μηδὲ γνόντο ἁμαρτίαν, ἀλλ' ἀποθανόντος ἐπὶ
τῇ καθαιρέσει οὐχὶ τῆς ἐν αὐτῷ ἁμαρτίας ἀλλὰ τῆς ἐν ἡμῖν, οὐχ οἷόν τε ἐστὶν
ἀποθανεῖν τινὰ τῶν ἡμαρτη κότων· πάντε δὲ ἥμαρτον καὶ ὑ τεροῦνται τῆ δόξη τοῦ
θεοῦ, δικαιούμενοι δωρεάν, καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. ἐν ἄλλοις δὲ λέγει· υνήγειρεν καὶ
υνεκάθι εν ἐν τοῖ ἐπουρανίοι ἐν Χρι τῷ· καὶ εἰ υνηγέρθητε τῷ Χρι τῷ, τὰ ἄνω
ζητεῖτε· πῶς οὖν ἐνταῦθα λέγει, καὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως ἐσόμεθα; πρὸς τοῦτο λεκτέον
ὅτι διττῶς ὀνομάζει τὴν ἀνάστασιν ὁ ἀπόστολος· μίαν μὲν τὴν ἤδη καθ' ἣν ὁ ἅγιος
συνανέστη Χριστῷ καὶ συνεγερθεὶς αὐτῷ τὰ ἄνω ζητεῖ· ἑτέραν δὲ τὴν ὅταν ἔλθῃ τὸ
τέλειον, περὶ ἧς καὶ ∆ανιὴλ προφητεύων φησὶν πολλοὶ τῶν καθευδόντων ἐν γῆ
χώματι ἀνα τή ονται, οὗτοι εἰ ζωὴν αἰώνιον, καὶ οὗτοι εἰ ὀνειδι μὸν καὶ εἰ αἰ χύνην
αἰώνιον· τὴν ἑτέραν μὲν οὖν τῶν ἀναστάσεων οἱ ἅγιοι ἐροῦσι συνεγηγέρθαι Χριστῷ,
κατὰ δὲ τὴν ἑτέραν καὶ ἀναστήσεσθαι. 30 vi 8–10 εἰ δὲ ἀπεθάνομεν σὺν Χριστῷ,
πιστεύομεν ὅτι καὶ συζήσομεν αὐτῷ· εἰδότες ὅτι Χριστὸς ἐγερθεὶς ἐκ νεκρῶν οὐκέτι
ἀποθνήσκει· θάνατος αὐτοῦ οὐκέτι κυριεύει· ὃ γὰρ ἀπέθανεν, τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ ἀπέθανεν
ἐφάπαξ· ὃ δὲ ζῇ, ζῇ τῷ θεῷ· οὕτως καὶ ὑμεῖς λογίζεσθε ἑαυτοὺς νεκροὺς μὲν εἶναι τῇ
ἁμαρτίᾳ, ζῶντας δὲ τῷ θεῷ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν. ἀποτετολμημένως
ἐπιφέρει τὸ θάνατος αὐτοῦ οὐκέτι κυριεύει, ὅπερ ἐστὶ δυσφημοειδές· οἱ γὰρ πλεῖστοί
φασιν ἀποθανεῖν αὐτὸν οὐ τῷ κυριεύεσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ θανάτου, ἀλλὰ τῷ ἑκόντα τὴν
ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ τεθεικέναι ὑπὲρ τῶν προβάτων ἑαυτοῦ, ἢ ὑπὲρ τῶν φίλων ἑαυτοῦ·
φησὶν γὰρ καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ σωτὴρ οὐδεὶ αἴρει τὴν ψυχήν μου ἀπ' ἐμοῦ ἀλλ' ἐγὼ τίθημι
αὐτὴν ἀπ' ἐμαυτοῦ. ὁ μὲν οὖν τις πρὸς ταῦτα φήσει ὅτι θάνατος λέγεται νῦν ὁ μέσος
καὶ ἀδιάφορος, ὃν κατὰ τὸ κοινότερον ἀπέθανεν ὅτε, ὥς φησιν ὁ Παῦλος, ἀπέθανεν
κατὰ τὰ γραφά . ἀλλὰ πῶς ταύτῃ δυνήσεται συναγορεῦσαι τῇ διηγήσει τὸ
ἀπεθάνομεν σὺν Χριστῷ, καὶ τὸ ὃ γὰρ ἀπέθανεν, τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ ἀπέθανεν ἐφάπαξ; ἀλλ'
pass_a_gloss: He died to sin once for all; and he, having died to sin, lives with Christ; and he lives with Christ who walks in newness of life. For the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us; for while we were still weak, Christ died at the right time for the ungodly. For scarcely will anyone die for a righteous person—though perhaps for a good person someone might even dare to die—but God demonstrates his own love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Much more then, having now been justified by his blood, we shall be saved through him from the wrath of God. Where he speaks of the weak or sinners, he names them and takes them to himself; but where he speaks of the ungodly, he does not. Perhaps it is fitting that the one under the law, who seeks by the strength of his own will, is weak and a sinner, yet not by the customary distinction of the Scriptures ungodly, as those under the law who sin against God are called; for if we sin, we who know the power—then the ungodly are those who are considered to be under the law and attain it, when, having forsaken the God of the fathers, they seek the gods of the nations. Before we came to God in reverence, love was not established in us; for we all loved something more than God. But when we were such, Christ died for us, and then the love of God was established and stood firm in us, after all things that hindered the establishment of God's love toward us were removed by the death of Jesus. According to this narrative, therefore, we ought to hear the establishing and establishing of God's love in us, which belongs to no one else properly except to God himself. (Origen) [For we do not only wait for immortal life, but also in the present life, as those who have become familiar with God, we are exalted, considering the things concerning the Lord Christ, who, having become our mediator, worked out peace.] If indeed we have become united with him in the likeness of his death, we shall certainly also be united with him in the likeness of his resurrection. He planted the name, having known a plant, namely the death of Jesus, bearing fruits that destroy sin; to which plant the word tills in those who have received the teaching through Christ, making them united with him in the likeness of his death. For a certain likeness of that death the human nature can take, but not his death, so as not to do sin, nor to know sin; but having died upon the cleansing, not of the sin in him, but of the sin in us, it is not possible for any of those who have sinned to die. But all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, being justified freely, and the rest. In other places he says: He raised up and made to sit in the heavenly places in Christ; and if you were raised with Christ, seek the things above. How then does he say here, and that we shall be in the resurrection? Let it be said that the apostle names the resurrection in two ways: one, namely that in which the holy one already rose with Christ and, having risen with him, seeks the things above; another, when the perfect comes, concerning which Daniel the prophet says, many of those sleeping in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, some to shame and everlasting contempt. The saints, therefore, say concerning the first resurrection that they have risen with Christ; but concerning the second, they shall rise again. If we died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him; knowing that Christ, having been raised from the dead, no longer dies; death no longer has dominion over him. For what he died, he died to sin once for all; and what he lives, he lives to God. So also you consider yourselves dead indeed to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord. He boldly brings forward that death no longer has dominion over him, which is disgraceful; for the most say that he died not in order to be ruled by death, but willingly gave up his soul for his sheep, or for his friends. For he himself, the Savior, says: No one takes my soul from me, but I lay it down of myself. Then someone might say on these matters that death is called now the middle and indifferent, which according to the common saying he died at that time, as Paul says, he died according to the Scriptures. But how can this be reconciled with the narrative that we died with Christ, and that what he died, he died to sin once for all?
pass_b_english: He endured death to sin in a single, definitive act; and he, having died to sin, now lives in communion with Christ. Indeed, the one who walks in newness of life walks with Christ. For the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who was given to us. This occurred precisely when we were still powerless: Christ died at the appointed moment for the ungodly. It is rare for someone to lay down their life for a righteous person—perhaps only for a genuinely good person might one find the courage to die. Yet God reveals his own love toward us in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Consequently, since we have now been justified by his blood, we shall be saved through him from the wrath of God. When the text speaks of the weak or sinners, it names them and draws them into communion; but when it refers to the ungodly, it does not name them. Perhaps this distinction reflects the condition of those who live under the law: they strive by their own strength, and thus remain weak and sinful, yet they are not labeled 'ungodly' in the ordinary scriptural sense—because those under the law who transgress against God are called sinners, not ungodly. The truly ungodly are those who, though they claim to live under the law and possess its knowledge, have abandoned the God of their ancestors and turned to the gods of the nations. Before we turned to God in reverence, love had not taken root within us, for we all loved something more than God. But in that very condition—while we were still such—Christ died for us, and only then was the love of God established and made firm within us, after every obstacle to its presence had been removed by the death of Jesus. From this we must therefore listen to the ongoing establishment and confirmation of God’s love within us, a love that belongs properly to none other than God himself. As we do not merely await immortal life, but even now, as those who have become acquainted with God, are exalted in our contemplation of the Lord Christ—who, having become our mediator, brought about peace—we are called to this awareness. Therefore, if we have truly been united with him in the likeness of his death, we shall most certainly also be united with him in the likeness of his resurrection. He planted a name, having come to know a certain plant—namely, the death of Jesus—which bears fruit that destroys sin. To this plant, the word tills among those who have received instruction through Christ, making them one with him in the likeness of his death. While human nature can assume a certain likeness of that death, it cannot take on his actual death, lest it fall into sin or even come to know sin. But having died—not to cleanse sin in himself, but to cleanse sin in us—no one who has sinned can die in that same way. For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, yet are justified freely, and the rest follows. In other passages, he says: God raised him up and seated him with himself in the heavenly realms in Christ; and if you have been raised with Christ, seek the things above. How, then, does he say here that we too shall be in the resurrection? Let it be understood that the apostle speaks of the resurrection in two ways: first, the resurrection in which the holy one has already risen with Christ and, having risen with him, now seeks the things above; second, the resurrection that will occur when the perfect comes—of which Daniel the prophet prophesied, saying that many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt. Thus, the saints affirm concerning the first resurrection that they have already risen with Christ; but concerning the second, they declare that they shall rise again. If we have died with Christ, we believe we shall also live with him, knowing that Christ, having been raised from the dead, no longer dies; death no longer holds dominion over him. For what he died to, he died to sin once for all; and what he lives for, he lives to God. So too, you should regard yourselves as truly dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord. He boldly affirms that death no longer rules over him—an idea that seems disgraceful to many, who claim he did not die to escape death’s rule, but willingly surrendered his soul for his sheep, or for his friends. For the Savior himself declares: No one takes my life from me; I lay it down of my own accord. Then someone might object, saying that death is now called the middle and indifferent state, as the common saying goes, that he died at that time, just as Paul says he died according to the Scriptures. But how can this be reconciled with the narrative that we died with Christ, and that what he died for, he died to sin once for all?

choices.issue: The nature of the ungodly in contrast to sinners under the law
choices.choice: The ungodly are those who, though under the law and knowledgeable of it, have forsaken the God of their fathers to serve foreign gods, while sinners under the law remain within the covenantal framework despite their transgressions.

choices.issue: The twofold meaning of resurrection in Pauline theology
choices.choice: The first resurrection refers to the present spiritual raising with Christ to seek heavenly things; the second points to the future bodily resurrection at the consummation, as foretold by Daniel, where some awaken to eternal life and others to contempt.
